title.narrative: Green Finance for Youth Employment (GFYE) Project

description.narrative:
The Project will target low-income rural young women and men aged between 18-35 years involved in both on-farm and off-farm activities in the Kenyan food system, including vulnerable groups, to provide them with improved prospects for decent and sustainable entrepreneurship and employment through green investments. The Project target group will be all youth and at least 50% young women in order to achieve the project's gender equality goals. The project will also target young Persons with Disability (PwD), however a target has not been set as further mapping will be required under the first component of the project, which will include identifying scalable green business models for young PwD. Based on the findings, the project will aim to reach a proportion of PwD with Technical Assistance (TA) and access to green finance through the other Project components
Direct Target Group: The Project will target approximately 8,000 young women and men, as well as 500 micro-, small- and medium enterprises (MSMEs), with the Project services. Cordaid will be responsible to target approximately 4000 young women and men and as well as 250 micro small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) Indirect Target Group: Indirectly, an additional estimated 10,000 youth will benefit from the Project as employees, producers and micro-entrepreneurs linked to the supported MSMEs.

The Project's goal is "Rural young women and men have increased and resilient incomes through green livelihoods". This goal will be pursued through achievement of two key outcomes: (i) Kenyan green finance ecosystem is improved with a taxonomy of scalable investment models suitable for youth, adopted by financial institutions and the government of Kenya, and (ii) The rural youth and rural enterprises access financing and operate sustainable investments for youth employment.

While the Kenyan economy has grown at a steady pace over the past few decades, youth unemployment remains a persistent challenge. According to the 2019 National Census, approximately 75% of Kenyans are under the age of 35. Among youth aged 18 to 34, the unemployment rate stands at 39%, compared to 10% in the general population. Notably, 80% of all unemployed individuals in Kenya are under 35. Young women face even steeper barriers, with an unemployment rate of 50%, compared to 30% among young men. Additionally, youth aged 18–25 experience the lowest levels of financial inclusion in the country, and rural-to-urban migration among young people is on the rise. To absorb this growing “youth bulge,” Kenya must create an estimated 900,000 new jobs annually. However, the potential demographic dividend remains largely untapped.
These challenges are compounded by the growing impacts of climate change, which are disproportionately affecting the agriculture sector—Kenya’s largest employer, supporting over 70% of the workforce. Climate-related hazards such as floods and droughts are projected to increase in frequency and intensity. Rising temperatures are expected to persist in the coming decades, further threatening rural livelihoods, reducing income-generating opportunities, and undermining the capacity of rural populations to repay loans—particularly those tied to agricultural activities.
The green economy offers a promising, yet underutilized, solution to address youth unemployment. It has significant potential to generate large numbers of jobs, especially in rural areas where the majority of the population resides. However, awareness among young people about green job opportunities—particularly along food system value chains and in climate-smart agriculture—remains low. Moreover, there is limited investment in the development and upgrading of climate- and environment-related skills among youth engaged in agriculture.
